title: After the Book
segs: Afterword. After the Book.

In September, a year and a half after the night she began, Anaya Deshmukh scrolled to the top of the decision log. (That is the notebook where she wrote down each big choice and why.) She read the first entry. It was dated 14 March. The decision was to work on the personal-details problem first and ticket themes second.
The evidence was a count. In one week, 37 of 400 conversations held an identity number, a tax number, a bank account or a full address. That was her own count, and Farah could check it.
She read the last line twice: "I would change my mind if". Of all the things the year had taught her, that line was the cheapest. It had done the most work.
Where the case ends.

By September the guard ran on every chat in two support teams. It was also in the trial of a lending partner. Behind Anaya, on the whiteboard, Imran had left a drawing in three colours. It showed everything that now stood between a customer's keyboard and the person who read the reply.

It had a shape for each thing the guard did. It had an arrow for each place where a decision was made. It had a star beside each place where a wrong answer would cost the most. It was not pretty. It was a true account of what had been built, like a map of a train line drawn by the people who laid the track.
What the seven parts add up to.
The book had seven parts. Each part added one kind of ability. Here they are in a table, like a checklist a reader can tick off.

Table 1: What a reader of each part should now be able to do. 1. The problem worth solving. Chapters: 1 to 7. The reader can: Turn an impression into a count, test an idea against the four product risks, learn from users by asking about the past, size a market from the bottom up, choose what not to do, plan in outcomes, and write a specification whose "done" can be tested. 2. Meeting the machine. Chapters: 8 to 13. The reader can: Say what a language model is and is not, read a request and its cost, explain why a chatbot's memory belongs to the application, write and test instructions, and measure with an answer key. 3. Finding things, and the whole machine. Chapters: 14 to 19. The reader can: Describe retrieval, choose where to cut documents, combine exact and meaning-based search, state recall and precision, and design output that a program can use. 4. Giving it work to do. Chapters: 20 to 26. The reader can: Let a model call tools within limits, budget what goes into a request, decide when reasoning is worth its cost, defend against injected instructions, grade at scale, and price a design honestly. 5. The messy real world. Chapters: 27 to 32. The reader can: Handle scans and speech, decide what may be sent to a vendor, document a system's limits, specify software that varies, choose between building and buying, and test whether a feature helps the business. 6. Under the hood. Chapters: 33 to 39. The reader can: Read the ordinary software around a model, choose a model on your own cases, review a retrieval system, bound an agent, release through a gate, and assume the worst. 7. A real product, and a job. Chapters: 40 to 47. The reader can: Turn a prototype into a service, price it, help people find it and stay, count what they do without recording what they write, work with the tools of a team, learn from real users, and show the work to an employer.
Eight sentences you can now say.
Each sentence below has a blank for a number from your own project. If you cannot fill one in yet, that is your next piece of work. It is not a reason to change the sentence.

I counted before I chose: N of N conversations in a week held an identity number. I can say what a model is and what it costs: one request of N tokens costs about N rupees, and the memory is held by my application. My retrieval finds the right passage N times in ten on my own questions, and I chose between recall and precision on purpose. My model uses tools within limits: N steps at most, and a person approves anything that cannot be undone. My specification has a threshold of N, and my pilot had a failure threshold that I wrote before it began. No change ships unless the gate passes on N rows, and I timed a rollback at N minutes. One message costs N rupees to serve, and the margin is N percent at base use. Here is what failed, N things, and here is the number that moved, from N to N.
What the project still does not know.

A textbook that ends in certainty has usually left something out. So here is what the guard had not been tested on. It was measured in English, in Hindi and in the mix of the two. The messages were ones the team had written itself. It was not measured in Tamil, Bengali or Telugu. It was not measured on the writing of customers outside two cities. It was not tested against an attacker with more patience than Imran.
Nobody who understood the word had called it compliant. It would be wrong for anyone to say so for it. It was a careful tool with honest numbers. That was all it had claimed to be.

The same care applies to the book. Sahaj, its people, its prices and its figures are made up. The tools and techniques are real. The failures are the kind that happen in real systems. Where a number matters, it shows how to reason about a number. Check it against your own cases before you borrow it.
Words.

Almost everything in this field has a name. Learning is hard partly because the names arrive faster than the things they stand for. It is like moving to a new city where every shop sign is in a language you are still learning. So each chapter brought in a few terms. Then it used them in the same sense in that chapter and every later one. The glossary at the back lists every term with a short meaning, and the chapter where it first appeared.
Using the book with the course app.

A book can give you the picture. It cannot give you the habit, and the habit is most of the skill. It is like cycling. Reading about it does not keep you upright. The material here becomes yours through practice. Write the plain description of a problem and find that it does not hold together. Build a small answer key and see how often you were wrong. Break a system on purpose and watch what it does.

The course app is built for that practice. Every chapter of the book has a partner in the app, linked beneath the chapter. It has the same ideas in the same order. It also has tasks to do and questions to answer and check. Read the chapter here, then do its work there. The course's weekly route follows that order. The two were written to be used together.

Please report it if the book and the course disagree. Please report it too if a term is used before it has been explained. The book was checked for exactly that, line by line. But a checker is no substitute for a reader.

You may be, as Anaya was, the person in the room who was asked to make sense of something nobody quite understands. If so, here is the advice. Begin a notebook with one line about what you noticed. Everything else follows from that.
